slides.title: WSB connects the competition workflow
slides.script: The original goal is to remove manual work in registration, payments, judging and tracking winners across WSB chapters. We now have connected local workflows for those tasks, with records and receipts instead of isolated form acknowledgements. This presentation shows what the implementation does today and where it still needs work. All demonstration data is synthetic. We are presenting a local implementation, not a production launch or a claim that every proposed feature is finished.
slides.transition: The design starts with the handoffs that create the paperwork.

slides.title: Paperwork fragments the event workflow
slides.script: The brief describes four administrative burdens: registering crews, tracking payment, collecting judging information and monitoring winners. When those live in separate records, staff have to carry information from one step to the next. The diagram represents that proposed problem, rather than a measured study of current WSB operations. Our response is to link the entry to its roster, payment state, score acceptance and deliberate publication. We still need an organizer pilot to measure the effect on workload and errors.
slides.transition: The first replacement is a registration workflow owned by WSB.

slides.title: Native registration keeps the roster connected
slides.script: Managers create a crew and invite dancers through our own forms. The entry selects canonical crew members, so the registrar reviews the same roster instead of a retyped copy. Commands preserve their original receipt when a response is lost. Submission can request corrections, and only authorized staff can approve an eligible entry. The app also owns contact, account support and chapter, studio or partner proposal conversations. A proposal receipt records intake; it does not grant affiliation. Guardian consent and actual music processing remain separate unfinished workflows.
slides.transition: Keeping forms inside the system also requires a private evidence boundary.

slides.title: Private evidence stays with authorized reviewers
slides.script: Identity and residency cases now have subject-owned upload paths and chapter-authorized human review. The backend checks object metadata and current authority, while private documents stay out of public results and development memory. This replaces an untracked document handoff with a recoverable case. It does not prove automated age eligibility, guardian authority or event waiver consent. Those need approved policy and additional implementation. File metadata checks also do not establish byte-level content safety or malware scanning.
slides.transition: Payment has the same principle: a request must not masquerade as a completed outcome.

slides.title: PayMongo simulation separates pending and paid
slides.script: PayMongo is the selected payment medium. Locally, the system reserves the available balance, creates or recovers a synthetic checkout, and waits for a signed synthetic event before crediting the ledger. Duplicate delivery must preserve one credit. Manual payment references and staff reconciliation also exist. Provider checkout, expiration, refund and signed webhook code has been introduced, but emulator tests do not prove live compatibility. The browser return page reads authoritative status. We still need controlled provider testing, including cancellation, refund dispatch failures and accounting recovery.
slides.transition: Judging likewise distinguishes a saved intention from server acceptance.

slides.title: Offline drafts wait for server acceptance
slides.script: An assigned judge can save a draft on a trusted device, review it and queue a versioned command. Reconnection sends the command to Rust, where current membership, assignment, version and division lock still apply. A receipt confirms acceptance; a conflict needs explicit resolution. This addresses lost connectivity without silently overwriting a newer score. Head-judge controls manage deductions, panel completeness and locking. The configured scoring policy used for local tests is synthetic. Offline judging does not imply that payments, stage commands or check-in work offline.
slides.transition: Accepted records then support event-day coordination.

slides.title: Versioned stage commands coordinate event staff
slides.script: Marshals use online roster check-in and a shared stage desk. Stage moves carry revisions, and the server checks approval, readiness, arrivals and stage assignment. Holds block new performance starts, while completion can release a running performance. Directors can create stages, assign marshals and change held, unoccupied configuration. Internal ordered drafts and their history make planning traceable. These drafts do not publish a schedule or enforce call order. The desk polls; it does not send push calls. Signed passes and offline arrival reconciliation remain unfinished.
slides.transition: The last handoff is the decision to make results public.

slides.title: Only published results reach spectators
slides.script: Private judging state and public results use different records. An authorized publication command requires the division lock and writes an immutable snapshot with a receipt. Spectators read that projection, so a provisional score is not automatically an announcement. This addresses the original winner-monitoring problem with an explicit release boundary. Tie handling, corrections, republication and advancement need approved rules and remaining workflow work. We should not infer that publishing results automatically qualifies crews for another event or issues certificates.
slides.transition: These workflows share one server authority and chapter boundary.

slides.title: Rust enforces the chapter boundary
slides.script: Next.js renders the website and operator workspaces. Rust owns business validation and chapter, event and stage authorization. Firestore transactions commit state with receipts and redacted audit in migrated workflows. Auth and Storage support identity and private files. Docker runs synthetic local services with mounted source and cached builds. Current business persistence is restricted to demo-wsb, and readiness deliberately remains closed. This architecture supports consistent recovery, but it is not evidence of production capacity, completed migrations or a deployed cloud system.
slides.transition: The release decision therefore depends on the work still to prove.

slides.title: The next milestone is an organizer pilot
slides.script: The implementation now demonstrates connected replacements for key paperwork tasks, but the full goal remains unfinished. The next milestone needs approved event and privacy rules, production identity and provider validation, guardian consent and music processing, passes, durable battles, advancement and HQ decisions. Then we can rehearse an entire event with organizers and measure completion time, reconciliation exceptions, score recovery and publication correctness. The appropriate conclusion today is a working local foundation with explicit release gates and a concrete pilot path.
slides.transition: The backup slides explain coverage, controls, evidence and the demonstration.

slides.title: Coverage extends beyond the main journey
slides.script: The core story focuses on the original administrative chain. The complete documentation also inventories public destinations, account workspaces, proposal intake, support recovery, private evidence, split-payment reservations, director stage controls and draft history. The open column is intentional: interface or route presence does not complete those domains.
slides.transition: For an exact boundary, consult the feature inventory.

slides.title: Retries preserve one authorized effect
slides.script: Authorization is checked again on retries and continuation pages. An old receipt or cursor does not restore revoked permission. An identical accepted operation recovers its original response, while altered payloads and stale versions conflict. The transaction commits the record, receipt and audit together. These are implemented patterns in migrated workflows, not a claim that every registered route has completed migration.
slides.transition: The evidence distinguishes these checks from production validation.

slides.title: Local evidence defines the current confidence
slides.script: For this documentation task, the running Docker services and HTTP liveness were checked directly. Workflow documents and memory record broader API, repository, browser, outbox and container-recovery checks. We did not rerun every suite while writing these materials. No measured time saving, live payment success or venue capacity is claimed. A 503 from readiness is deliberate: liveness and partial persistent operation do not imply release readiness.
slides.transition: The short demonstration stays inside that evidence boundary.

slides.title: A 90-second demo follows one entry
slides.script: Prepare a synthetic unpaid entry and sign in before starting. Show its native entry and quote, create and settle a labeled local checkout, reload and confirm its saved paid state. Do not switch roles or attempt a full event in ninety seconds. If local payment controls are unavailable, show a previously rehearsed saved synthetic receipt and explicitly call it a recorded result. The full guide contains exact actions, prerequisites and a fallback plan.
slides.transition: Open the system manual for the full operational procedures and remaining scope.
